Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) screen titles and abstracts without review-specific training, but
generating screening decisions as text takes processing time and incurs API charges. We evaluated
Jev, a non-generative model returning classification probabilities, on 4527 records from two
systematic reviews of bipolar disorder treatments. We used human reviewers’ decisions to retain
records for full-text assessment as the reference standard. In the primary analysis, we asked Jev
yes-or-no questions (“Noul”) about whether to retain each record. Records were retained when their
retention probability was at least 50%, a cutoff specified before the final evaluation runs. We also
evaluated lower retention thresholds. For comparison, we gave Jev explicit include/exclude options
(“Choice”) and used the same prompts with GPT-5 mini and GPT-6 Astra; both LLMs used default
reasoning. In the primary analysis at 50%, sensitivity and specificity were 99.6% and 98.9% for
light therapy and 93.2% and 93.5% for adjunctive pharmacotherapy. Lower cutoffs selected on these
data retained all reference-positive records. Compared with assessing every record manually, these
cutoffs reduced the

adjunctive pharmacotherapy. For light therapy and adjunctive pharmacotherapy, sensitivity was
92.3% and 90.0% with Jev using explicit options at 50%, 87.2% and 90.0% with GPT-5 mini, and
92.3% and 80.8% with GPT-6 Astra. Costs for screening all 4527 records once were US$0.20 for Jev
using explicit options, US$2.59 for GPT-5 mini, and US$33.45 for GPT-6 Astra. Jev's probabilities
could provide graded information for reviewers assessing titles and abstracts.

Highlights
What is already known
Generative LLMs can screen titles and abstracts using natural-language eligibility criteria, but generating each
decision takes time and incurs API charges.
What is new
Jev screened records without generating text or requiring training on records labeled for each review. In two
reviews, screening cost substantially less than with the tested LLM configurations.
Potential impact for Research Synthesis Methods readers
Rather than providing only an include-or-exclude decision, Jev indicates how strongly the model favors
retaining each record. Reviewers could consider this information alongside the title, abstract, and eligibility
criteria.
Keywords: systematic reviews; title and abstract screening; machine learning; large language models;
probability thresholds; workload reduction.

1. Introduction
Clinical practice guidelines depend on systematic reviews, which take a long time to
produce,1 and title and abstract screening accounts for much of the workload. With earlier machinelearning classifiers, records were ranked by a relevance score, but training required labeled records
from each review.2,3 Large language models (LLMs) can screen titles and abstracts using eligibility
criteria written in natural language, without training on records labeled for the individual review.
Title and abstract screening is now conducted with LLMs, and recent evidence syntheses reported
high sensitivity.4,5 Although routine use of LLMs has been judged premature,6 combining judgments
from several models or pairing an LLM with a human reviewer performed well,7,8 and
implementation has already extended to national clinical guideline production.9
Screening, however, is a classification task performed through text generation with
generative LLMs. Outputs are decisions rather than scores10-12 and LLM confidence is often poorly
calibrated.13-15 Errors also occur: eligible studies were excluded under some screening conditions
with GPT-5, a previous frontier model from OpenAI.16 In

calibrated.13-15 Errors also occur: eligible studies were excluded under some screening conditions
with GPT-5, a previous frontier model from OpenAI.16 In addition, generating each screening
decision and any intermediate reasoning token by token takes processing time and incurs API
charges.17-19 The cost of screening a fixed set of records can be lowered by sending multiple records
to the LLM in each request (batching). However, increasing the number of records per request has
been reported to reduce sensitivity or produce invalid outputs in some models.20
Jev, a recently introduced non-generative model developed by TypeSafe AI and described by
its developer as a System One model, processes natural-language input and returns probabilities for
specified answers without generating text token by token.21,22 According to TypeSafe AI, Jev
evaluates multiple questions about the same input in parallel, so asking additional questions has
little effect on the time needed to return a response.22 For screening, several records can be placed
in the shared input, with a separate question asking whether to retain each record. This
arrangement could reduce the

in the shared input, with a separate question asking whether to retain each record. This
arrangement could reduce the time and cost of screening a fixed set of records. Like an LLM, Jev
does not require training on records labeled for each review. It also provides a score for each record,

Although Jev has shown task-dependent probability calibration when used to judge
generated responses,23 its screening performance and the correspondence between its probabilities
and human retention decisions remain untested in systematic reviews. We evaluated Jev on two
datasets from our previous study of title and abstract screening10 and compared Jev with two
generative LLMs using the same prompts. We examined sensitivity, the number of records requiring
human review, and probability calibration against human retention decisions. We also assessed
whether performance was maintained as the number of records per request increased, and
measured latency, processing time, and cost.

2. Methods
2.1. Study design, datasets, and reference standard
We analyzed two datasets previously used to evaluate GPT-3.5 and GPT-410: 1381 records
from a systematic review of bright light therapy for bipolar disorder (hereafter, light therapy)24 and
3146 from a systematic review of adjunctive pharmacotherapy for bipolar depression.25 Eligibility
criteria

review of bright light therapy for bipolar disorder (hereafter, light therapy)24 and
3146 from a systematic review of adjunctive pharmacotherapy for bipolar depression.25 Eligibility
criteria are described in the source reviews,24,25 and human screening procedures in our previous
study.10 The original records had been screened in duplicate by pairs of human evaluators. Their
decisions formed the basis of the reference standard; records retained for full-text assessment are
referred to as human-retained records. In our previous study, records retained by human reviewers
but excluded by GPT were reassessed. When exclusion was judged appropriate, the reference label
was changed to excluded. We incorporated 13 adjudicated exclusions and resolved three additional
labels: a related open-label report, a discrepancy between source sheets, and a missing consensus
label. Reference labels were then fixed before the final evaluations.10 The final reference standard
comprised 26 human-retained records for light therapy and 87 for adjunctive pharmacotherapy.

2.2. Jev and prompts
A Jev request contains the content to be evaluated, termed the state, and one or more
questions. Each question consists of instructions and a question type. The questions are evaluated
against the same state independently and in parallel, and each receives an answer in the format
specified by its type, without text generation. Figure 1 summarizes the screening approaches and
study design. We used two question types. A “Noul” question asks for a yes-or-no judgment and
returns a single value from 0 to 1: the probability of yes. A “Choice” question presents a set of
options and returns a probability for each option; these probabilities sum to 1.21-23 We accessed jev-
1.13.0 through the TypeSafe API on September 18, 2026 (UTC).
The primary analysis used Noul questions.22 We used GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI) as an agent in
a separate Codex session to draft screening criteria from the two source reviews,24,25 without giving
GPT-6 Astra access to screening records, reference labels, earlier prompts, or screening results. The
criteria specified that records with uncertain eligibility should be retained and clearly incompatible
records excluded. Each request's state

labels, earlier prompts, or screening results. The
criteria specified that records with uncertain eligibility should be retained and clearly incompatible
records excluded. Each request's state contained the criteria and one or more records, with an
identifier for each record. One Noul question per record asked whether that record should be
retained for full-text assessment. We treated the returned value as the probability of retention.
The secondary analysis used Choice questions.22 We adapted the prompts from our previous
study10 to assess study design, population, intervention, and comparator together, with include and
exclude as the options. Each request's state contained one record, and the instructions contained the
criteria and query. We used the probability assigned to include as the probability of retention. The
complete prompts are provided in Figure S1.

study, Jev was run 10 times under each condition to characterize run-to-run variability. The
primary analysis used one record per request, and we repeated it with up to 10, 25, or 50 records

2.4. Comparison with generative LLMs
We accessed GPT-5 mini (gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07) and GPT-6 Astra (gpt-6-astra) through the
OpenAI API on September 19, 2026 (UTC). Each request contained one record, followed by the
criteria, query, and response options of the secondary analysis and an instruction to answer with
the single letter I or E.10 We ran GPT-5 mini with the lowest accepted reasoning setting (minimal)
and the default setting (reasoning effort unspecified), and GPT-6 Astra with the default setting.

Previous studies set the temperature to 0 to reduce variability in outputs,10 but the API did not
accept a temperature setting for either model. We therefore ran each condition three times, with up
to 50 concurrent requests. For all models, request latency covered dispatch to the parsed response,
excluding pacing and retry waits. Run processing time included pacing, rate-limit waits, and retries.
Costs were calculated from token usage in saved successful responses at the study list prices,
including LLM reasoning tokens as output tokens. Setup calls and unobserved usage from failed
requests were excluded. Time and token usage were counted once per request when records were
bundled.

3.2. Human retention according to model-assigned probability
In both datasets and both analyses, no record assigned a probability below 10% was
human-retained in any run. Among light-therapy records with probabilities of 60 to 100%, the mean
percentage of human-retained records was 83.4% in the primary analysis and 93.6% in the

at most 4.9% in any interval below 60%. The percentage increased across the four intervals from
60% to 100%, reaching 85.9% in the primary analysis and 69.2% in the secondary analysis in the
highest interval, 90 to 100% (Figure 2).

4. Discussion
In these reviews, Jev screened titles and abstracts without generating text or training on
records labeled for each review. Jev Choice used the same prompts as the LLMs; at the prespecified
cutoff, its sensitivity and specificity were similar to or higher than those of the LLMs with default
reasoning, and its cost was lower. Like earlier classifiers trained for individual reviews,2,3 Jev
provides a graded score for each record. Jev can do so using eligibility criteria written in natural
language.
Jev's low screening cost warrants comparison with GPT-5 mini as another low-cost
screening option. Previous studies have reported high but imperfect LLM screening sensitivity;5,27,28
our earlier GPT-based study also documented exclusions of human-retained records.10 Even with
minimal reasoning, GPT-5 mini cost more than Jev Choice. Moreover, it excluded reports ultimately
included in both source reviews. Default reasoning improved sensitivity and retained all ultimately
included reports from the adjunctive-pharmacotherapy review, but the same light-therapy report

may already be at a level sufficient to replace a single human reviewer, although further research is
needed because its performance may depend on domain knowledge that varies across fields. Another
potential advantage is that, Jev's probability output indicates how strongly the model favors
retaining a record. While it does not establish eligibility or substitute for human judgment on final

retaining a record. While it does not establish eligibility or substitute for human judgment on final
inclusion,32 reviewers could consider this graded information alongside the title, abstract, and
eligibility criteria when assessing a record.
Processing time also matters when screening must be repeated after searches are
updated.33 With one record per request, Jev returned individual responses faster than the LLMs.
However, the total time to screen all records was similar because Jev requests were spaced to stay
within its API limit. Sending multiple records per request reduced the total time to seconds. All Jev
runs completed successfully, whereas invalid outputs have been reported for some generative LLMs
with larger batches.20 Of note, compared with sending one record per request, sending multiple
records lowered sensitivity for adjunctive pharmacotherapy at the fixed cutoff and increased
variation in probabilities across runs. Given that screening with one record per request already
completed within a practical time frame, sending multiple records per request may not be necessary

when sensitivity is prioritized.

bipolar disorder, limiting generalizability to other clinical areas. The datasets also contained few

5. Conclusions
Across the two systematic reviews evaluated, Jev achieved high screening sensitivity at the
prespecified cutoff, retained all reports included after full-text assessment, and cost less than the
tested LLM configurations. External validation is needed, as this study used only the datasets from
our previous evaluation. System One models such as Jev are likely to play a central role in title and
abstract screening for future systematic reviews. The emergence of additional models in this class
